```{r libraries, message = FALSE}
library(nlmixr2lib)
library(rxode2)
library(PKNCA)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

Zhu R, Poland B, Wada R, Liu Q, Musib L, Maslyar D, Cho E, Yu W, Ma H, Jin JY,
Budha N. *Exposure-response-based product profile-driven clinical utility
index for ipatasertib dose selection in prostate cancer.* CPT Pharmacometrics
Syst Pharmacol. 2019;8(4):240. doi:10.1002/psp4.12394.

Zhu 2019 relates the exposure of ipatasertib, an oral AKT inhibitor, to
radiographic progression-free survival (rPFS) and to diarrhea and rash in the
randomised phase II part of the A.MARTIN study, then combines the projected
dose-responses in a clinical utility index (CUI) that supported the 400 mg
once-daily phase III dose. The paper contributes ten landmark models to the
library: a logistic regression for each of four adverse-event endpoints and a
Cox regression for rPFS, each fitted on two exposure metrics.

* `AUC_IPAT_EVT` -- the steady-state daily AUC from the average **actual**
  dose up to the event (source `AUCss,event`, the primary metric). Dose
  interruptions and reductions are folded in.
* `AUC_IPAT_SS` -- the steady-state daily AUC at the **nominal** dose (source
  `AUCss`, the exploratory metric). Models on this metric carry the suffix
  `_nominal`.

Both are the daily dose divided by the individual apparent clearance of an
ipatasertib population PK model, in ng\*h/mL. None of the ten models has a PK
layer or an ODE: exposure is a data column.

# Population

All 253 randomised patients of the A.MARTIN phase II study (NCT01485861)
contributed: men with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer after
docetaxel, randomised 1:1:1 to ipatasertib 400 mg (n = 84), 200 mg (n = 87)
or placebo (n = 82) once daily, each with abiraterone 1000 mg and prednisone
10 mg daily (Zhu 2019 Methods, Study design; Results). Placebo patients enter
every regression with zero exposure. Dose modifications, mostly for adverse
events, occurred in 14.6%, 14.9% and 39.3% of the placebo, 200 mg and 400 mg
arms. Age, weight and race are not reported in Zhu 2019; the primary trial
publication is de Bono 2019 (Clin Cancer Res 25:928).

# The ten models

```{r models}
er_models <- tibble::tribble(
  ~model, ~output, ~exposure, ~source, ~endpoint,
  "diarrhea_grade2", "prob_diarrhea_grade2", "AUC_IPAT_EVT", "Table S2", "Diarrhea, grade >= 2",
  "diarrhea_grade3", "prob_diarrhea_grade3", "AUC_IPAT_EVT", "Table S2", "Diarrhea, grade >= 3",
  "rash_grade2", "prob_rash_grade2", "AUC_IPAT_EVT", "Table S2", "Rash, grade >= 2",
  "rash_grade3", "prob_rash_grade3", "AUC_IPAT_EVT", "Table S2", "Rash, grade >= 3",
  "rpfs", "hr", "AUC_IPAT_EVT", "Table S1", "rPFS hazard ratio vs placebo (Cox)",
  "diarrhea_grade2_nominal", "prob_diarrhea_grade2", "AUC_IPAT_SS", "Table S2", "Diarrhea, grade >= 2",
  "diarrhea_grade3_nominal", "prob_diarrhea_grade3", "AUC_IPAT_SS", "Table S2", "Diarrhea, grade >= 3",
  "rash_grade2_nominal", "prob_rash_grade2", "AUC_IPAT_SS", "Table S2", "Rash, grade >= 2",
  "rash_grade3_nominal", "prob_rash_grade3", "AUC_IPAT_SS", "Table S2", "Rash, grade >= 3",
  "rpfs_nominal", "hr", "AUC_IPAT_SS", "Table S1", "rPFS hazard ratio vs placebo (Cox)"
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(model = paste0("Zhu_2019_ipatasertib_", model))

mods <- lapply(setNames(er_models$model, er_models$model), function(m) {
  rxode2::rxode(readModelDb(m))
})

er_models |>
  dplyr::rename(
    "Model" = model, "Output" = output, "Exposure column" = exposure,
    "Source" = source, "Endpoint" = endpoint
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "The ten exposure-response models from Zhu 2019.")
```

The logistic models return `prob_<endpoint> = expit(logit_ref + e_auc_logit *
AUC)`; the Cox models return the hazard ratio versus placebo, `hr =
exp(e_auc_haz * AUC)`. A Cox regression leaves the baseline hazard
unspecified, so no survivor function is available.

# Source trace

| Quantity | Value(s) | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Logistic form `logit(P) = alpha + beta * AUC` | -- | Equation beneath Table S2; Methods, E-R analysis (R `glm`, binomial, logit link) |
| Cox form `lambda(t) = lambda0(t) * exp(beta * AUC)` | -- | Equation beneath Table S1 |
| `logit_ref`, `e_auc_logit` (8 logistic models) | see table below | Table S2 |
| `e_auc_haz` (2 Cox models) | -0.0000739 (actual dose), -0.0000488 (nominal) | Table S1 |
| Exposure unit, ng\*h/mL | -- | x-axis of Figures 3 and S3 |
| Exposure definitions | -- | Methods, Response and exposure data; Additional exploratory E-R analysis |
| Dose-intensity model form (Eqs. 1-2) | -- | Methods, DI modeling |
| Dose-intensity coefficients (5 endpoints) | see table below | digitised from Figure S2 |
| CUI attributes, cut-offs and weights | -- | Table 1; Results |
| Population counts and dose modifications | -- | Methods, Study design; Results |

```{r tables2}
  "rash_grade2_nominal", "logit_ref", -5.73, 0.932, -7.89, -4.17,

  "rpfs_nominal", "e_auc_haz", -0.0000488, 0.0000549, -0.000156, 0.0000588
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(model = paste0("Zhu_2019_ipatasertib_", model))

pub$packaged <- mapply(function(m, p) {
  idf <- mods[[m]]$iniDf
  idf$est[idf$name == p]
}, pub$model, pub$param, USE.NAMES = FALSE)
# Wald half-width implied by the printed SE, relative to the printed CI
# half-width (the CIs are profile-likelihood intervals, so they are mildly
# asymmetric on the intercepts).
pub$ci_over_wald <- ((pub$hi - pub$lo) / 2) / (qnorm(0.975) * pub$se)

pub |>
  dplyr::mutate(model = sub("Zhu_2019_ipatasertib_", "", model)) |>
  dplyr::rename(
    "Model" = model, "Parameter" = param, "Estimate" = est, "SE" = se,
    "CI lower" = lo, "CI upper" = hi, "Packaged value" = packaged,
    "CI half-width / (1.96 SE)" = ci_over_wald
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 7, caption = "Zhu 2019 Tables S1 and S2 against the packaged models.")

stopifnot(
  # Every packaged coefficient is exactly the printed estimate.
  isTRUE(all.equal(pub$packaged, pub$est)),
  # Each estimate sits inside its own CI, and each CI half-width agrees
  # with its SE to within 15%: a mistyped estimate, SE or bound fails here.
  all(pub$est > pub$lo & pub$est < pub$hi),
  all(abs(pub$ci_over_wald - 1) < 0.15)
)
```

# Exposure-response curves (Figures 3a-b and S3)

```{r er-eval}
# Evaluate a packaged model at a vector of exposures: one observation row
# per value, exposure supplied as the covariate column.
er_eval <- function(model, output, cov_name, auc) {
  ev <- data.frame(id = 1L, time = seq_along(auc), amt = 0, evid = 0L)
  ev[[cov_name]] <- auc
  s <- as.data.frame(rxode2::rxSolve(model, events = ev, returnType = "data.frame"))
  stopifnot(nrow(s) == length(auc))
  s[[output]]
}
row_of <- function(m) er_models[er_models$model == m, ]
eval_model <- function(m, auc) {
  r <- row_of(m)
  er_eval(mods[[m]], r$output, r$exposure, auc)
}

grid <- seq(0, 7000, by = 50)
curves <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(er_models$model[!grepl("rpfs", er_models$model)], function(m) {
  r <- row_of(m)
  tibble::tibble(
    model = m, endpoint = r$endpoint, exposure = r$exposure,
    auc = grid, p = eval_model(m, grid)
  )
}))

ggplot(curves, aes(auc, p, colour = exposure)) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~endpoint) +
  labs(
    x = "Ipatasertib steady-state daily AUC (ng*h/mL)", y = "Probability",
    colour = "Exposure metric",
    caption = "Replicates the model curves of Figure S3 (AUC_IPAT_EVT) and Figure 3a-b of Zhu 2019."
  )
```

Figure 3 draws the grade >= 2 diarrhea curves out to 6600 ng\*h/mL, where they
end at about 0.88 (actual-dose metric, panel a) and 0.81 (nominal-dose metric,
panel b); both curves start near 0.05 at zero exposure.

```{r fig3-check}
fig3 <- c(
  evt = eval_model("Zhu_2019_ipatasertib_diarrhea_grade2", c(0, 6600)),
  ss = eval_model("Zhu_2019_ipatasertib_diarrhea_grade2_nominal", c(0, 6600))
)
round(fig3, 3)
stopifnot(
  abs(fig3[["evt2"]] - 0.88) < 0.02,
  abs(fig3[["ss2"]] - 0.81) < 0.02,
  abs(fig3[["evt1"]] - 0.05) < 0.01
)
```

# Dose-intensity model (Figure S2)

To project a nominal dose onto `AUC_IPAT_EVT`, Zhu 2019 fits an
endpoint-specific dose-intensity (DI) model (Methods, Eqs. 1-2): DI is the
total dose up to the event divided by the treatment duration and the nominal
dose. A logistic regression gives `P(DI >= 1)`, and the logit of DI among
patients with DI < 1 is normal:

* `logit(P(DI >= 1)) = Intercept1 + Slope1 * Dose`
* `logit(DI | DI < 1) = Intercept2 + Slope2 * Dose + eps`, `eps ~ N(0, sigma^2)`

The paper prints no coefficients. The values below were digitised by the
maintainers from the raster panels of Figure S2 (one logit-linear fit across
every pixel column of each drawn curve, R `lm`). The left-panel regression lines
are reproduced with a residual SD of 0.003 on the logit scale, which confirms
the form. In the right panels the drawn central curve is `expit(mu)` and the
lower edge of the 90% band is `expit(mu - 1.645 * sigma)`. The two run
parallel on the logit scale (the sigma implied at low and at high doses agrees
within 1.5% in every panel), which is what a constant sigma predicts.

```{r di-model}
di <- tibble::tribble(
  ~endpoint, ~panel, ~int1, ~slope1, ~int2, ~slope2, ~sigma,
  "rpfs", "A", -0.0642, -0.002175, 3.3906, -0.003240, 1.856,
  "diarrhea_grade2", "B", 0.1593, -0.001898, 3.8542, -0.003929, 1.703,
  "diarrhea_grade3", "C", 0.2261, -0.003365, 3.7616, -0.004279, 1.810,
  "rash_grade2", "D", 0.2449, -0.003044, 3.7949, -0.003866, 1.813,
  "rash_grade3", "E", 0.2220, -0.003059, 3.7340, -0.003759, 1.796
)
di |>
  dplyr::rename(
    "Endpoint" = endpoint, "Figure S2 panel" = panel,
    "Intercept1" = int1, "Slope1 (1/mg)" = slope1,
    "Intercept2" = int2, "Slope2 (1/mg)" = slope2, "sigma" = sigma
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 6, caption = "Dose-intensity coefficients digitised from Zhu 2019 Figure S2.")

di_curves <- tidyr::crossing(di, dose = seq(0, 500, by = 10)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    p_full = plogis(int1 + slope1 * dose),
    di_median = plogis(int2 + slope2 * dose),
    di_lo = plogis(int2 + slope2 * dose - qnorm(0.95) * sigma)
  )
ggplot(di_curves, aes(dose)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = p_full, linetype = "P(DI >= 1)")) +
  geom_line(aes(y = di_median, linetype = "Median DI given DI < 1")) +
  geom_line(aes(y = di_lo, linetype = "5th percentile DI given DI < 1")) +
  facet_wrap(~endpoint) +
  labs(
    x = "Nominal dose (mg)", y = NULL, linetype = NULL,
    caption = "Replicates the fitted curves of Zhu 2019 Figure S2."
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

# Exposure generator

The population PK model behind both exposure metrics (two compartments,
first-order absorption, relative bioavailability increasing with dose) is not
printed in Zhu 2019. As a stand-in, exposures here are generated from the
published Yoshida 2021 ipatasertib model (`Yoshida_2021_ipatasertib`), fitted to
five phase I and II studies that include A.MARTIN, with abiraterone
co-administration and the multiple-dose bioavailability step switched on. Its
steady-state daily AUC is `1000 * F * Dose / (CL/F)`, linear in dose.

PKNCA first confirms that this closed form is what the ODE model delivers
over a dosing interval at steady state (typical patient: 64 years, 75 kg, with
abiraterone; day 14 of once-daily dosing).

```{r pk-check}
pk_full <- rxode2::rxode(readModelDb("Yoshida_2021_ipatasertib"))
th <- setNames(pk_full$iniDf$est, pk_full$iniDf$name)
pk <- rxode2::zeroRe(pk_full)
auc_per_mg_typ <- 1000 * exp(th[["lfdepot"]]) * (1 + th[["e_md_fdepot"]]) /
  (exp(th[["lcl"]]) * (1 + th[["e_abi_cl"]]))

doses_pk <- c(200, 400)
dose_times <- seq(0, 13 * 24, by = 24)
obs_times <- sort(unique(c(seq(312, 336, by = 0.25), seq(0, 312, by = 6))))
ev_pk <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(seq_along(doses_pk), function(i) {
  d <- doses_pk[[i]]
  dplyr::bind_rows(
    data.frame(id = i, time = dose_times, amt = d, evid = 1L, rate = -2, cmt = "depot"),
    data.frame(id = i, time = dose_times, amt = d, evid = 1L, rate = -2, cmt = "depot_m1"),
    data.frame(id = i, time = obs_times, amt = 0, evid = 0L, rate = 0, cmt = "central")
  ) |>
    dplyr::mutate(
      treatment = paste(d, "mg QD"), AGE = 64, WT = 75, CONMED_ABI = 1,
      # The model has two endpoints (parent Cc and metabolite); dvid = 1
      # maps these observation rows to the parent.
      dvid = ifelse(evid == 0L, 1L, NA_integer_)
    )
})) |>
  dplyr::arrange(id, time, dplyr::desc(evid))

sim_pk <- as.data.frame(rxode2::rxSolve(pk, events = ev_pk, keep = "treatment", returnType = "data.frame"))

conc <- sim_pk |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(Cc)) |>
  dplyr::select(id, time, Cc, treatment) |>
  dplyr::bind_rows(data.frame(id = seq_along(doses_pk), time = 0, Cc = 0, treatment = paste(doses_pk, "mg QD"))) |>
  dplyr::distinct(id, time, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  dplyr::arrange(id, time)
doses_df <- ev_pk |>
  dplyr::filter(evid == 1L, cmt == "depot") |>
  dplyr::select(id, time, amt, treatment)

o_conc <- PKNCA::PKNCAconc(conc, Cc ~ time | treatment + id)
o_dose <- PKNCA::PKNCAdose(doses_df, amt ~ time | treatment + id)
ints <- data.frame(start = 312, end = 336, auclast = TRUE, cmax = TRUE)
nca <- PKNCA::pk.nca(PKNCA::PKNCAdata(o_conc, o_dose, intervals = ints))
nca_tab <- as.data.frame(nca$result) |>
  dplyr::filter(PPTESTCD == "auclast") |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    closed_form = auc_per_mg_typ * as.numeric(sub(" mg QD", "", treatment)),
    pct_diff = 100 * (PPORRES - closed_form) / closed_form
  )
nca_tab |>
  dplyr::select(treatment, PPORRES, closed_form, pct_diff) |>
  dplyr::rename(
    "Treatment" = treatment, "PKNCA AUC(day 14) (ng*h/mL)" = PPORRES,
    "1000 * F * Dose / (CL/F) (ng*h/mL)" = closed_form, "Difference (%)" = pct_diff
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 1, caption = "Steady-state daily AUC of the typical patient: ODE versus closed form.")
stopifnot(all(abs(nca_tab$pct_diff) < 3))
```

The two agree within about 2%, with the same percentage at both doses, as a
model linear in dose requires.

The virtual cohort is a deterministic grid of 200 quantiles of the lognormal
individual AUC per mg implied by the Yoshida 2021 between-subject variances on
CL/F and F, so the projections below involve no random numbers. For the
actual-dose models each patient is split by the DI model: with probability
`P(DI >= 1)` the patient keeps the nominal exposure, otherwise the exposure is
scaled by DI drawn on a grid of 40 quantiles of the logit-normal DI
distribution. This mirrors the paper's simulation (Methods, Dose-response
projections), which used 1000 replicates of 1000 random patients.

```{r cohort}
n_pk <- 200L
n_di <- 40L
z_pk <- qnorm(((1:n_pk) - 0.5) / n_pk)
z_di <- qnorm(((1:n_di) - 0.5) / n_di)
# log(AUC) = log(F) - log(CL/F) + const, so its variance is the sum of the
# two independent Yoshida 2021 variances.
auc_per_mg <- auc_per_mg_typ * exp(sqrt(th[["etalcl"]] + th[["etalfdepot"]]) * z_pk)
summary(auc_per_mg * 400)

# Mean model output over the cohort at a nominal dose. `scale` multiplies
# every patient's exposure (1 = the Yoshida 2021 exposures).
project <- function(m, dose, scale = 1) {
  r <- row_of(m)
  auc_nom <- dose * auc_per_mg * scale
  if (r$exposure == "AUC_IPAT_SS") {
    return(mean(eval_model(m, auc_nom)))
  }
  d <- di[di$endpoint == sub("Zhu_2019_ipatasertib_", "", m), ]
  p_full <- plogis(d$int1 + d$slope1 * dose)
  di_part <- plogis(d$int2 + d$slope2 * dose + d$sigma * z_di)
  out <- eval_model(m, c(auc_nom, as.vector(outer(auc_nom, di_part))))
  full <- out[seq_len(n_pk)]
  part <- rowMeans(matrix(out[-seq_len(n_pk)], nrow = n_pk))
  mean(p_full * full + (1 - p_full) * part)
}
```

# Dose-response projections (Figures 1 and 2)

The model-predicted central values of Figures 1 and 2 (grey triangles) were
read from the published figures by the maintainers.

```{r projections}
fig_pred <- tibble::tribble(
  ~model, ~dose, ~published,
  "rpfs", 200, 0.913, "rpfs", 300, 0.86, "rpfs", 400, 0.80, "rpfs", 500, 0.77,
  "diarrhea_grade2", 0, 0.05, "diarrhea_grade2", 200, 0.12, "diarrhea_grade2", 300, 0.25,
  "diarrhea_grade2", 400, 0.41, "diarrhea_grade2", 500, 0.56,
  "diarrhea_grade3", 0, 0.01, "diarrhea_grade3", 200, 0.03, "diarrhea_grade3", 300, 0.08,
  "diarrhea_grade3", 400, 0.17, "diarrhea_grade3", 500, 0.28,
  "rash_grade2", 0, 0.004, "rash_grade2", 200, 0.02, "rash_grade2", 300, 0.08,
  "rash_grade2", 400, 0.21, "rash_grade2", 500, 0.37,
  "rash_grade3", 0, 0.002, "rash_grade3", 200, 0.02, "rash_grade3", 300, 0.06,
  "rash_grade3", 400, 0.18, "rash_grade3", 500, 0.35
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(model = paste0("Zhu_2019_ipatasertib_", model))

proj <- fig_pred |>
  dplyr::rowwise() |>
  dplyr::mutate(yoshida = project(model, dose)) |>
  dplyr::ungroup()

proj |>
  dplyr::mutate(model = sub("Zhu_2019_ipatasertib_", "", model)) |>
  dplyr::rename(
    "Model" = model, "Dose (mg)" = dose, "Zhu 2019 Figure 1/2" = published,
    "Projected, Yoshida 2021 exposures" = yoshida
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3, caption = "Projected rPFS hazard ratio and adverse-event probabilities by nominal dose.")

stopifnot(
  # At 400 mg, the dose the stand-in PK model and the source PK model agree
  # on, every adverse-event projection is within 0.05 of the published one.
  with(dplyr::filter(proj, dose == 400, !grepl("rpfs", model)), all(abs(yoshida - published) < 0.05))
)
```

At 400 mg the projections agree with the published ones. At 200 and 300 mg
they run high and at 500 mg slightly low, the signature of the dose-dependent
relative bioavailability of the paper's own PK model, which the linear
Yoshida 2021 model lacks: the source model gives lower exposure than a linear
model below 400 mg and higher above it.

## Cross-check with exposure calibrated to Figure 1

The rPFS hazard ratio of Figure 1 depends on the PK only through the exposure
it is evaluated at. Solving, at each dose, for the factor on the Yoshida 2021
exposures that reproduces the Figure 1 hazard ratio recovers the exposure the
paper's PK model delivered. Feeding the same factor to the four adverse-event
models then predicts Figure 2 with no reference to Figure 2, so agreement
tests all four logistic transcriptions together with the DI model.

```{r calibrated}
scale_fig1 <- vapply(c(200, 300, 400, 500), function(dz) {
  target <- fig_pred$published[fig_pred$model == "Zhu_2019_ipatasertib_rpfs" & fig_pred$dose == dz]
  stats::uniroot(function(s) project("Zhu_2019_ipatasertib_rpfs", dz, s) - target, c(0.2, 3))$root
}, numeric(1))
names(scale_fig1) <- c(200, 300, 400, 500)
round(scale_fig1, 3)

cal <- fig_pred |>
  dplyr::filter(!grepl("rpfs", model), dose > 0) |>
  dplyr::rowwise() |>
  dplyr::mutate(calibrated = project(model, dose, scale_fig1[[as.character(dose)]])) |>
  dplyr::ungroup()

cal |>
  dplyr::mutate(model = sub("Zhu_2019_ipatasertib_", "", model)) |>
  dplyr::rename(
    "Model" = model, "Dose (mg)" = dose, "Zhu 2019 Figure 2" = published,
    "Projected, exposure calibrated to Figure 1" = calibrated
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3, caption = "Adverse-event projections with exposure calibrated to the rPFS hazard ratios of Figure 1.")

stopifnot(
  # The implied exposure rises with dose relative to a linear model.
  scale_fig1[["200"]] < scale_fig1[["300"]], scale_fig1[["300"]] < scale_fig1[["400"]],
  # Over the studied and interpolated doses all four endpoints match.
  with(dplyr::filter(cal, dose <= 400), all(abs(calibrated - published) < 0.05))
)
```

The calibrated exposure rises faster than dose from 200 to 400 mg, as the
paper's dose-dependent bioavailability requires, and every adverse-event
projection from 200 to 400 mg then lands within 0.035 of the published
value. At 500 mg, outside the studied doses, the projections fall short of
Figure 2. The Figure 1 hazard ratio flattens between 400 and 500 mg (0.80 to
0.77) and its confidence band is very wide there, so the factor solved at
500 mg is poorly determined.

## Projections

```{r projection-plot}
dose_grid <- c(0, 100, 200, 300, 400, 500)
proj_all <- tidyr::crossing(model = er_models$model, dose = dose_grid) |>
  dplyr::filter(!(grepl("rpfs", model) & dose == 0)) |>
  dplyr::rowwise() |>
  dplyr::mutate(value = project(model, dose)) |>
  dplyr::ungroup() |>
  dplyr::left_join(er_models, by = "model")

ggplot(proj_all, aes(dose, value, colour = exposure)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  geom_point(
    data = dplyr::left_join(fig_pred, er_models, by = "model"),
    aes(dose, published), colour = "black", shape = 2, inherit.aes = FALSE
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~endpoint, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(
    x = "Nominal ipatasertib dose (mg once daily)", y = "Probability, or hazard ratio vs placebo",
    colour = "Model exposure metric",
    caption = "Lines: projections with Yoshida 2021 exposures. Triangles: Zhu 2019 Figures 1 and 2."
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

The nominal-dose models need no DI model. Zhu 2019 reports that the two
metrics give similar dose-response projections (Figure 3c-d, Figure S4).

# Clinical utility index (Table 1)

The CUI is a weighted sum of linear utilities that equal 0 at the minimal and
1 at the optimistic product profile of each attribute (Methods, Benefit-risk
analysis). Scenario 2 weights the rPFS hazard ratio 0.6, grade >= 3 diarrhea
0.3 and grade >= 3 rash 0.1. Because the utilities are linear, the expected
CUI is the CUI of the expected attributes, so it can be evaluated directly at
the projections; the paper's CUI distributions (10th-90th percentiles, Figure
4b) also propagate the projection uncertainty, which is not repeated here. The
efficacy attribute uses the Figure 1 hazard ratios and the safety attributes
the projections calibrated to them. Figure 4a values were read from the
published figure by the maintainers; "Safety" is the diarrhea-plus-rash
utility `(0.3 * U_diarrhea + 0.1 * U_rash) / 0.4`.

```{r cui}
util <- function(x, x0, x1) (x - x0) / (x1 - x0)
cui <- tibble::tibble(dose = c(200, 300, 400, 500)) |>
  dplyr::rowwise() |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    hr = fig_pred$published[fig_pred$model == "Zhu_2019_ipatasertib_rpfs" & fig_pred$dose == dose],
    d3 = project("Zhu_2019_ipatasertib_diarrhea_grade3", dose, scale_fig1[[as.character(dose)]]),
    r3 = project("Zhu_2019_ipatasertib_rash_grade3", dose, scale_fig1[[as.character(dose)]]),
    safety = (0.3 * util(d3, 0.20, 0.10) + 0.1 * util(r3, 0.15, 0.05)) / 0.4,
    cui = 0.6 * util(hr, 0.73, 0.65) + 0.4 * safety
  ) |>
  dplyr::ungroup() |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    fig4a_safety = c(1.50, 1.12, 0.20, -1.18),
    fig4a_cui = c(-0.78, -0.47, -0.47, -0.75)
  )
cui |>
  dplyr::rename(
    "Dose (mg)" = dose, "rPFS HR" = hr, "P(diarrhea grade >= 3)" = d3,
    "P(rash grade >= 3)" = r3, "Safety utility" = safety,
    "Safety utility, Figure 4a" = fig4a_safety,
    "CUI, scenario 2" = cui, "CUI, Figure 4a" = fig4a_cui
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3, caption = "Scenario 2 expected clinical utility index (Zhu 2019 Table 1 and Figure 4a).")

stopifnot(
  # The expected CUI from 200 to 400 mg reproduces Figure 4a, including its
  # near-equal maximum at 300 and 400 mg.
  with(dplyr::filter(cui, dose <= 400), all(abs(cui - fig4a_cui) < 0.1))
)
```

From 200 to 400 mg the expected CUI reproduces Figure 4a: it rises from 200 to
a near-equal maximum at 300 and 400 mg, all values below 0 because the
projected rPFS hazard ratio never reaches the minimal product profile of 0.73.
At 500 mg the safety utility is less negative than in Figure 4a, a consequence
of the 500 mg adverse-event projections falling short of Figure 2 (above).

# Assumptions and deviations

* **No PK layer.** Each model takes its exposure as a data column. The paper's
  own population PK model (two compartments with dose-dependent relative
  bioavailability) is not printed, so the projections above use the published
  Yoshida 2021 model as a stand-in. Because that model is linear in dose, it
  over-predicts exposure at 200-300 mg and under-predicts it at 500 mg relative
  to the source model; the Figure 1 calibration quantifies the difference.
* **Dose-intensity model digitised.** Zhu 2019 prints the DI model form but no
  coefficients; the values were digitised from Figure S2 and are used only in
  this article to project nominal doses onto `AUC_IPAT_EVT`. They are not part
  of the packaged models.
* **Published projections read from figures.** The Figure 1 and Figure 2
  central values, and the Figure 3 curve end points, were read from the raster
  figures to about 0.01.
* **No residual error.** The logistic regressions have a Bernoulli
  likelihood. Each logistic model carries a fixed placeholder additive
  residual SD of 0.001 on the probability so that rxode2 has an error model;
  it is not a published quantity. The Cox models declare no endpoint.
* **No baseline hazard.** The Cox models return the hazard ratio versus
  placebo only; the semiparametric fit has no baseline hazard to package.
  Both rPFS relationships are not statistically significant (P = 0.232 and
  0.374).
* **Exposure units.** Tables S1 and S2 give no unit; ng\*h/mL is the x-axis
  unit of Figures 3 and S3, and the coefficients reproduce those curves.
* **Endpoint names.** `prob_rash_grade3` is registered with this paper as its
  founding example; the diarrhea and grade >= 2 rash outputs reuse existing
  canonical names.
